clinicalPearls: A ranula that extends beyond the floor of mouth into the neck, presenting as a soft submandibular or upper cervical swelling
Occurs when extravasated saliva from the sublingual gland tracks around or through a dehiscence in the mylohyoid muscle into the neck
May present as a painless neck mass with or without an obvious oral floor-of-mouth component, sometimes fluctuating in size
Like the oral ranula, it is usually a pseudocyst lacking a true epithelial lining and formed by extravasated mucus
MRI or CT characterises the cystic lesion and its cervical extension, and a tail extending toward the sublingual space supports the diagnosis
Aspiration yields viscous, amylase- and protein-rich mucoid fluid, helping distinguish it from other cystic neck lesions
Definitive treatment addresses the source by excising the sublingual gland, which resolves the cervical component without needing separate neck dissection of the pseudocyst
Simple drainage or excision of the neck cyst alone is associated with high recurrence
reference.pathophysiology: A plunging ranula is a variant of the sublingual gland mucus extravasation lesion in which mucus escapes into the neck rather than remaining confined to the floor of the mouth. Saliva leaking from a disrupted sublingual gland tracks posteriorly and inferiorly around the free posterior edge of mylohyoid, or through a congenital or acquired dehiscence within the muscle, descending into the submandibular and upper cervical spaces. The collection is a pseudocyst without a true epithelial lining, and because the sublingual gland continues to secrete, definitive resolution depends on removing that gland to stop the flow of mucus.
additionalDifferentials: Thyroglossal duct cyst when near the midline
Dermoid cyst or abscess of the neck
additionalInvestigations: MRI or CT of the neck and floor of mouth to define the cyst and its sublingual connection
Ultrasound to characterise the cystic lesion and guide aspiration
Aspiration demonstrating viscous, amylase-rich mucoid fluid
Histological examination of the excised sublingual gland and any cyst wall
Assessment for an associated oral ranula component
redFlags: Large or rapidly enlarging neck swelling causing airway or swallowing concern
Features atypical for a pseudocyst suggesting a neoplastic or vascular lesion
Signs of secondary infection with pain, erythema and systemic upset
Recurrence after previous surgery indicating retained sublingual gland tissue
reference.prognosis: Excision of the offending sublingual gland gives a high cure rate and resolves the cervical component. Procedures that drain or remove only the neck pseudocyst while leaving the gland in place commonly recur.
pitfalls: Treating the visible neck cyst without removing the sublingual gland, leading to recurrence
Misdiagnosing the mass as another cystic neck lesion and pursuing inappropriate surgery
Failing to recognise the connection to the sublingual space on imaging
Injuring the lingual nerve or submandibular duct during sublingual gland excision
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Definitive treatment is transoral excision of the offending sublingual gland to stop the mucus extravasation
Removal or marsupialisation of the cervical pseudocyst alone is inadequate and prone to recurrence, so gland excision is required
Aspiration or drainage may temporarily decompress a large collection but is not curative
Careful surgical technique to protect the lingual nerve, submandibular duct and gland during excision
Histological examination of the excised gland and cyst wall to confirm the diagnosis and exclude other cystic neck lesions
Otolaryngology and head-and-neck surgical referral for operative planning with imaging correlation
Postoperative monitoring for recurrence and for any residual oral floor-of-mouth ranula component
